[[File:Polygraph (mathematics).svg|thumb|380px|A polygraph with 0-cells (vertices), 1-cells (gray edges), 2-cells (red edges), and 3-cells (blue edges). The red shading indicates a path of two 1-cells (''a'', ''b'') that together form the source of a 2-cell. This can be done for the source and/or target of any dimension (where applicable, 0-cells can't be connected, and so 0 and 1-cells can't show this property), as long as the set is a path (tip-to-tail) such as cells ''a'' and ''b''.]]

{{Short description|Higher-dimensional generalized digraph}}
{{About|a notion of higher-dimensional directed graph|the forensic instrument|Polygraph|the dual pen device that produces a simultaneous copy of an original while it is written in [[cursive writing]]|Polygraph (duplicating device)|an author that can write on a variety of different subjects|Polygraph (author)}}

In [[mathematics]], and particularly in [[category theory]], a '''polygraph''' is a generalisation of a [[directed graph]].  It is also known as a '''computad'''.  They were introduced as "polygraphs" by [[Albert Burroni]]<ref>A. Burroni. ''Higher-dimensional word problems with applications to equational logic''. TCS, 115(1):43--62, 1993.</ref> and as "computads" by [[Ross Street]].<ref>R. Street. Limits indexed by category-valued 2-functors. Journal of Pure and Applied Algebra, 8(2):149--181, 1976.</ref>

In the same way that a [[Multigraph#Directed_multigraph_(edges_without_own_identity)|directed multigraph]] can [[Free object|freely]] generate a [[Category (mathematics)|category]], an ''n''-computad is the "most general" structure which can generate a free [[n-category]].<ref name="nlab_c">{{nlab|id=computad}}</ref>

In the context of a graph, each dimension is represented as a set of '''<math>k</math>-cells'''. Vertices would make up the 0-cells, edges connecting vertices would be 1-cells, and then each dimension higher connects groups of the dimension beneath it. For 2-cells and up, which connect edges themselves, a source or target may consist of ''multiple'' edges of the dimension below it, as long as each set of elements are '''composites''', i.e., are paths connected tip-to-tail.<ref name="nlab_c"/>

A [[globular set]] can be seen as a specific instance of a polygraph. In a polygraph, a source or target of a <math>k</math>-cell may consist of an entire path of elements of (<math>k</math>-1)-cells, but a globular set restricts this to singular elements of (<math>k</math>-1)-cells.<ref name="nlab_c"/><ref name="nlab_g">{{nlab|id=globular+set}}</ref>
